title: Multiplayer agentic engineering — Arjun Singh, Superconductor
talk_summary: Arjun Singh describes how his team (ex-GradeScope, now Superconductor) integrated agents into every human interface, moved all agent work into isolated cloud sandboxes, and benchmarked models on their own codebase to stay model-agnostic. The core message is that agentic engineering works best when agents are untethered from laptops, visible/collaborative across the team, and routed by measured cost/quality on your own tasks rather than public benchmarks.

takeaways.technique: Benchmark models on your own codebase via real PRs
takeaways.what_they_do: Select PRs representing good engineering work (agent, human, or hybrid), run each candidate model/harness against them, and plot quality vs cost and quality vs time on their own repo.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we select pull requests that represent great engineering work... You pick the agents you want to use and benchmark.
takeaways.numbers: 3,300 Claude Code runs cost $10,000 in tokens daily (on plans, so not actually paid); Codex had 4x as many sessions and was cheaper overall; 1.5B tokens in a month

takeaways.what_they_do: Keep the workflow decoupled from any single model so a new best model (or a model being taken away) can be swapped in without disrupting the team; default model changed to Codex based on benchmark data, then briefly to a new model, then back.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The best model and harness can change weekly... you don't want that to disrupt your entire team's flow.

takeaways.technique: Isolated cloud sandboxes with configurable network egress
takeaways.what_they_do: Run all agent work in cloud sandboxes (not laptops), grant only needed credentials, and enforce a configurable network allow/deny list that prompts for access on a per-ticket or per-project basis.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you have a configurable network sandbox and you say, 'Look, these are the places you're allowed to access, these are the ones you can't access.'

takeaways.technique: One shared agent session across all interfaces
takeaways.what_they_do: The same agent session/context is reachable from Slack, app, GitHub, etc., so a human can ask the agent a question mid-review without waiting for the original author, and artifacts (screenshots/video) are visible everywhere.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the exact same agent session... the agent didn't forget what you did in one place in Slack when you go and talk to it from GitHub

takeaways.what_they_do: A meeting bot and other ingestors listen to calls/Slack/bug trackers, dedupe against existing work (link instead of duplicate), and auto-create and start tickets with acceptance criteria.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If it finds existing work, it'll link to it... It created this ticket and started working on it.
takeaways.numbers: dozens of new ideas prototyped per call; 'at least a few shippable PRs with a very minimal intervention'

takeaways.technique: Human review retained on top of agent review
takeaways.what_they_do: Even with ~99.9% agent-generated PRs, every change is still human-reviewed, with agents assisting the review.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We know that quality and reliability and security are really important, so we still have humans look at everything.
takeaways.numbers: 99.9% of PRs heavily agent generated; still 100% human reviewed
